country: Soviet Group of Forces in Cuba (Operation Anadyr)
person: General Issa Pliyev, commander of the Group of Forces (code name Pavlov)
card: Headquarters at El Chico, southwest of Havana. 22–28 October · 8 decisions. Twenty-four missile launchers and their nuclear warheads are under your command, Moscow is eight hours ahead, and orders come only by coded cable.
intro: You are Issa Aleksandrovich Pliyev, 58, a cavalry commander from Ossetia who led a cavalry-mechanized group in the war and is twice a Hero of the Soviet Union. On 6 July 1962 the Presidium named you commander of the Soviet Group of Forces in Cuba, and on paper you go by the name “Pavlov.” Moscow sent a ground-forces general rather than a rocket-forces general for the sake of cover. Under you are Major General Statsenko’s 51st Missile Division (24 R-12 launchers), two air-defense divisions, four ground-forces regiments, three battalions of Luna tactical rockets, a regiment of FKR cruise missiles, a squadron of Il-28 bombers, and the nuclear warheads in Colonel Beloborodov’s keeping. Soviet troops number about 42,000 in all. Your deputies at hand are Lieutenant General Grechko for air defense and Major General Garbuz for combat training, and in Havana Ambassador Alekseev passes on what Castro says. In Moscow, Defense Minister Malinovsky sends his coded cables under the name “Trostnik.” A draft instruction in September would have let you use tactical nuclear weapons at your own discretion, but it was never signed, and that fact comes back again and again over these seven days.

PL-01.time: About 4 p.m. (11:30 p.m. in Moscow, 5 p.m. in Washington)
PL-01.place: Headquarters of the Soviet Group of Forces in Cuba, El Chico, southwest of Havana
PL-01.title: No. 4/389
PL-01.clock: About two hours until Kennedy’s speech (6 p.m. Havana)

map.caption: The R-12 regiments were deployed at San Cristóbal in the west and Sagua la Grande in the center, R-14 sites were being built at Guanajay, and the headquarters of the Group of Forces was at El Chico, southwest of Havana.

telegram.subject: Raising combat readiness
telegram.text: In connection with a possible landing in Cuba by American forces now on maneuvers in the Caribbean, take urgent measures to raise combat readiness and to repel the enemy by the joint efforts of the Cuban army and all Soviet units. / Excepting Statsenko’s means and all of Beloborodov’s cargo.

PL-01.event: Ambassador Dobrynin in Washington has told Moscow that President Kennedy will make a major speech at 7 p.m., Washington time. The Kremlin convened the Presidium at 10 p.m. and put off its decision until the text arrives at 1 a.m., but sent you an order on combat readiness first. Havana does not yet know about the speech, and in New York the United States, Cuba and the Soviet Union are about to request a meeting of the Security Council.
PL-01.scene: You are in the commander’s office at El Chico when the cipher clerk brings in the decoded cable. It is an order of fewer than ten lines: a possible American landing, combat readiness to be raised, the enemy to be repelled jointly with the Cubans. And in the last line, fixed in place: “Excepting Statsenko’s means and all of Beloborodov’s cargo.” Statsenko’s means are the R-12 medium-range missiles; Beloborodov’s cargo is the nuclear warheads. In other words, even if the landing comes, you are to fight with conventional weapons alone. This is not what you heard in September. Then you were told that an instruction was being prepared under which, if landing forces came ashore and communications with Moscow were cut, the commander could decide on his own to use the nuclear means of the Lunas, the FKRs and the Il-28s; that document never came with a signature on it. Statsenko comes in with a report on the division’s readiness. Sidorov’s regiment finished its preparations on 20 October, and Bandilovsky’s regiment and the 2nd Battalion of Solovyov’s regiment are nearly done. No one knows what Kennedy will say in two hours, but the cable is already here.

voices.text: Comrade Commander, Sidorov’s regiment is ready to carry out its mission. Bandilovsky and Solovyov’s 2nd Battalion will be done in two days. I will take the division to heightened combat readiness. But the warheads are in storage, and under this cable they stay there.

voices.who: Garbuz (deputy commander for combat training, recalling in 1992)
voices.text: We were told it was forbidden to use the nuclear warheads of the FKR and Luna missiles or of the aircraft without Moscow’s approval.

The two air-defense divisions have 24 S-75 battalions. Without permission to switch on the radars, we are sitting here with our eyes shut. Landing or air strike, if we want to see before we shoot, we have to switch them on in advance.

choices.text: Cable Moscow asking under what conditions the nuclear means may be used. Prepare as ordered, but get an answer on the Lunas and FKRs in the event of a landing
choices.why: You cannot meet a landing holding an ambiguous order
choices.after: The cable went out, but no answer came. Moscow spent that night waiting for the text of the speech and the next day wrestling with the blockade. Your question would come back to you only five days later, in another form.

choices.text: Carry out the order as written: Statsenko’s division to heightened combat readiness, conventional units to prepare to repel the enemy with the Cubans, and the nuclear means left untouched
choices.why: If Moscow has drawn a line, you prepare to fight inside it
choices.after: Overnight the Group of Forces went to combat readiness. At 5:40 a.m. on 23 October Castro put all forces on alert and declared a state of war, and Cuban radio repeated the substance of Kennedy’s speech. At 8 a.m. Statsenko’s division reported “heightened combat readiness.”

choices.text: Put the whole Group of Forces on maximum alert and have the missile division time its launch preparations too. Read the order broadly
choices.why: If the landing comes, there will be no time to receive new orders
choices.after: Statsenko began timing each regiment’s launch preparations: Sidorov’s regiment 10 hours, the others 14–16. The figures went up on the headquarters wall, and no one asked whether they matched what Moscow intended.

note.text: No. 4/389 explicitly excluded the nuclear means. At the Moscow Presidium at 10 p.m. that night Khrushchev spoke of letting “tactical atomic weapons” be used “if there is an airborne assault,” but Malinovsky stopped him: “wait until 1 a.m., or we will give them grounds to use atomic weapons.” It did not go into the order. The 8 September instruction delegating tactical nuclear use in advance exists only as a single handwritten draft, and Malinovsky did not sign it. General Gribkov claimed in 1992 that the authority had been delegated, but most historians hold that no valid delegation existed on paper.
note.src: Wilson 117316; Malin 10/22; NSA CMC 620908; Phase 1 issue 1

pressure.title: The Unsigned Document
pressure.text: The last line of No. 4/389 nails it down: all of Statsenko’s means and Beloborodov’s cargo are excluded. The instruction you heard about in September, the document that would have let the commander decide on nuclear means himself in the event of a landing and a communications breakdown, never came with a signature, and now your orders say the opposite. You do not know that at the Moscow Presidium that same night Khrushchev raised the idea of letting tactical nuclear weapons be used if there were an airborne assault, and that Malinovsky stopped him by saying they should wait until 1 a.m. You are a cavalry commander; a missile division and nuclear warheads are new charges for you. Four months ago, in your district, troops opened fire on their own country’s workers, yet Moscow sent you to Cuba without asking you to answer for it. Whether you become a commander who reads his orders narrowly or one who reads them broadly is settled on this first night.

PL-02.time: About 8 p.m. (4 a.m. on the 25th in Moscow, 9 p.m. in Washington)
PL-02.place: Operations room, Group of Forces headquarters, El Chico
PL-02.title: Fighters at a Hundred Meters
PL-02.clock: Eleven hours since the quarantine line took effect (9 a.m. Havana); about eleven hours until the next low-level reconnaissance (morning of the 25th)
PL-02.event: At 11:30 a.m. on 23 October two American fighters passed over the missile regiments at 100–150 meters. The launchers and fuel trucks must have come out clearly in their photographs. At 10 a.m. on the 24th, Washington time, the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba) took effect, and before that Moscow had already turned back 16 ships. Castro has moved 50 anti-aircraft batteries from Havana to protect the missile units, and Ambassador Alekseev has reported to Moscow that the Cuban forces are under orders to fire “only if the enemy begins the attack.”
PL-02.scene: Statsenko has spread out a map. After yesterday’s overflight he decided to pick new launch areas for every regiment. Launchers whose positions the Americans know will vanish in the first hour of an air strike, so his idea is to move them at night and fire from places they do not know. He also means to issue an order tonight detaching equipment and men from Sidorov’s regiment to bring Solovyov’s regiment up to full strength in a hurry. But Garbuz has come with other numbers. Moving the launchers needs spare parts for the SP-6 transporters, and there are not enough. A launcher that breaks down on the road will be standing in daylight under American reconnaissance planes. Fifty Cuban anti-aircraft batteries have moved in around the division, but their commanders are under orders not to fire unless attacked first. You must decide whether to move the division, keep it where it is and hide it, or do something about the sky.

voices.text: Yesterday they counted our launchers. If an air strike comes, they will hit the places they know first. If we move to new launch areas at night, we save the first salvo. Stripping Sidorov’s equipment to fill out Solovyov also has to be done tonight.
Comrade Commander, we have no SP-6 spare parts. If one launcher stops on the road, it gets photographed on that road in the morning. Moving is easy. Stopping halfway is the problem.

voices.who: Alekseev (ambassador to Cuba, cable of 22–23 October)
voices.text: The troops have been ordered to open fire on enemy aircraft and ships only if the enemy begins the attack.

choices.text: Hold your present positions. Movement only raises the risk of being spotted, so thicken the camouflage and keep the division behind the 50 batteries the Cubans have moved in
choices.why: A hidden launcher lives longer than a moving one
choices.after: The division stayed put and the camouflage nets multiplied. The next day the American reconnaissance planes came in along the same route and photographed the same launchers. Even the extra camouflage showed up in the pictures.

choices.text: Ask the air-defense divisions to return fire on low-level flights. The next plane that comes in at a hundred meters gets driven off with anti-aircraft guns
choices.why: A soldier’s instinct: whoever gets photographed gets hit first
choices.after: Grechko stood a long while holding the order. He still had no permission to switch on his radars, and an order to fire had come first. The next morning one battery fired a few rounds at a low-flying plane, which escaped out to sea untouched. How those few rounds appeared in whose reports, you never learned.

choices.text: Approve Statsenko’s plan to move. Pick new launch areas, and at night shift equipment and men from Sidorov’s regiment to Solovyov’s
choices.why: You cannot take the first salvo in places the Americans already know
choices.after: Overnight Sidorov’s equipment went to Solovyov’s regiment. The move to new launch areas was put off for lack of SP-6 spare parts; Statsenko looked for an alternative on the 25th and reported it on the 26th. Two days later the decision to withdraw would make that report useless.

note.text: Statsenko’s report of December 1962 records the low pass at 11:30 on 23 October, the decision on the 24th to change launch areas, and its postponement for lack of SP-6 spare parts. The shift of 50 Cuban anti-aircraft batteries appears in Castro’s letter of 28 October. American low-level photographic reconnaissance began on 23 October.

PL-03.time: About 9 a.m. (5 p.m. in Moscow, 10 a.m. in Washington)
PL-03.place: El Chico headquarters, from the signals room to the commander’s office
PL-03.title: The Aleksandrovsk
PL-03.clock: 24 Soviet ships stopped outside the blockade line; one ship inside a north-coast port in Cuba

telegram.subject: The 665th and 668th Regiments and the Aleksandrovsk
telegram.text: In view of U.S. Navy blockade of approaches to Cuba, decided not to send you 665th and 668th Missile Regiments. / Do not unload R-14 warheads from transport Aleksandrovsk. If already unloaded, reload secretly onto Aleksandrovsk. / Report readiness of Aleksandrovsk to sail.

PL-03.event: That morning the Presidium in Moscow (protocol No. 61) decided on “the return of the ships carrying special cargo” and settled the line of its reply to Kennedy: remove the missiles in exchange for a promise to leave Cuba alone. That line was not passed to you. What reached you was an order about one ship.
PL-03.scene: The Aleksandrovsk is the ship that was ordered on 23 October to make for “the nearest port” and put into a harbor on Cuba’s north coast. In her holds are 24 nuclear warheads for the R-14 medium-range missiles and warheads for the FKR cruise missiles; the R-14 missiles themselves turned back outside the blockade line. There is no reason to unload warheads that have no missiles, but Colonel Beloborodov thinks it more dangerous to leave a ship full of nuclear warheads tied up at a quay in the middle of a blockade. If the Americans announce they will search ships entering port, he says, she could be the first. The cable has come “personal.” You have three paths: leave the warheads aboard as ordered and report her ready to sail; unload them at night, move them to storage, and report the unloading already complete; or move the ship to Mariel and put her under the protection of what is to become a Soviet naval base.

voices.who: Beloborodov (colonel, in charge of nuclear warhead storage and escort)
voices.text: Comrade Commander, warheads on a ship belong not to me but to the sea. If the blockade line reaches into the harbor, that ship will be the first one searched. If we unload at night and take them to storage, at least they will be on land.
The cable is marked “personal.” What Moscow is asking the commander, and him alone, is whether the ship can sail. Nowhere does it say to unload.
The news that the ships have turned back is shaking the Cuban leadership. Castro asks why he was not told. If word gets out that even the warhead ship is going home, it will be harder still.

choices.text: As ordered, keep the R-14 warheads aboard, make the ship ready to sail, and report her readiness in No. 8/162
choices.why: An order that comes “personal” is the commander’s to carry out as written
choices.after: The Aleksandrovsk stayed at the quay and made ready to sail. On 27 October Moscow answered your report No. 8/162: “Send the Aleksandrovsk to the Soviet Union together with the Bratsk.” The 24 R-14 warheads never touched Cuban soil.

choices.text: Unload the warheads at night, move them to the Group’s storage, and report that the unloading was already complete. Putting a ship to sea in the middle of a blockade is the greater danger
choices.why: On the ground’s reckoning, warheads can be guarded only on land
choices.after: The warheads came off at night and went into storage. Moscow sent “reload secretly” again, and you bought a few days. Which way Moscow’s decision went in those few days would decide the fate of those warheads.

choices.text: Move the ship to Mariel, under the guard of the base the submarine brigade is to use, and wait there for sailing orders
choices.why: A compromise: if you must wait, wait somewhere you can defend
choices.after: The ship moved along the coast to Mariel at night. An American patrol plane photographed the voyage in daylight, and Washington learned that one Soviet ship had changed ports. Why, it did not learn.

note.text: The Aleksandrovsk carried 24 R-14 warheads and 44 FKR warheads (Malin notes, translator’s note 29), and the Indigirka, which reached Mariel on 4 October, had already brought in 36 R-12 warheads, 36 FKR warheads, 12 Luna warheads and 6 Il-28 bombs (NSA EBB 449). The FKR warheads on the two ships add up to 80, which matches Savranskaya’s count (2012) and the figures in the withdrawal order of 20 November (80 FKR, 12 Luna, 6 bombs). Garbuz testified to “183,” strategic and tactical together. The original of the 25 October cable is in the Wilson Center Digital Archive. The cable does not name the port the ship entered, so it is not named here.

PL-04.time: About 8 p.m. (4 a.m. on the 27th in Moscow, 9 p.m. in Washington)
PL-04.place: El Chico headquarters, air-defense command post
PL-04.title: Radar
PL-04.clock: About eight hours until the air strike the Cubans expect (dawn on the 27th)
PL-04.event: In Moscow, at 4:43 p.m. Moscow time, Khrushchev’s long letter was delivered to the American embassy: a letter asking that neither side pull on the knot of war. You know nothing of it. What you know is the word from Ambassador Alekseev: the Cuban leadership expects an air strike between tonight and tomorrow, and Castro has decided to open anti-aircraft fire if the attack comes. From today Statsenko’s division is allowed to switch on its radar surveillance system.
PL-04.scene: For the first time the screens in the air-defense command post are lit. With the radars on after five days dark, the American reconnaissance flights over Cuba are drawn as lines: several times a day they come in low, cut across the island and leave over the sea. Grechko reports on his 24 S-75 battalions. All ready to fire. The problem is the order. No. 4/389 said to “repel the enemy jointly with the Cuban army,” and it does not say whether repelling includes air-defense fire. Castro has said the Cuban anti-aircraft guns will fire tonight. If the Cubans fire and the Soviets stay silent, it is no alliance; if the Soviets fire, theirs will be the first Soviet missile to bring down an American plane. It is 8:34 p.m., and Garbuz is waiting for an order to fire. How to word that order, and what cable to send Moscow, are yours to decide.

voices.text: The radars are on. The order to fire has to come from you, Comrade Commander. If we get it after the attack starts, the first bombs will already have fallen. If you tell us to fire without warning on aircraft crossing the border, it will reach every battalion tonight.

voices.who: Garbuz (deputy commander for combat training, recalling in 1992)
voices.text: We received an order to fire without warning on aircraft crossing the border.
Castro thinks the air strike will come tonight or tomorrow. The Cubans will fire if they are attacked. He is asking what the Soviet forces will do, and I must give him your word, Comrade Commander.

choices.text: Do not wait for the attack. Order both air-defense divisions to fire without warning on every aircraft that crosses the border
choices.why: Reconnaissance planes are the eyes of an air strike, so put out the eyes first
choices.after: The order reached every battalion before morning. Low-flying planes came in beneath the S-75’s minimum altitude and were the Cuban guns’ business; high altitude belonged to your missiles. When a high-altitude reconnaissance plane entered the sky the next morning, the battalion commanders had nothing left to ask.

choices.text: Switch on all the radars, decide to answer an American attack with every air-defense means, and report this to Moscow. The nuclear ban stands
choices.why: An ally’s reckoning: on a night when the Cubans fire, the Soviets cannot stay silent
choices.after: A cable went to Moscow: the Cubans expected a night air strike, Castro had decided on anti-aircraft fire if attacked, and the Group of Forces too had decided to use all air-defense means if attacked. No air strike came that night. Morning came with the decision to fire still standing.

choices.text: Switch on the radars but forbid firing until Moscow gives permission. Even if the Cuban guns fire, Soviet air defense stays silent
choices.why: The moment the first Soviet missile splits the sky is for Moscow to choose
choices.after: Grechko took the order down, his face set. Word went out to the battalion commanders to track only and keep the launchers locked. No air strike came that night, and the next morning something else was in the sky.

note.text: Statsenko’s report states that permission to operate the radars dated from 26 October. Pliyev’s cable of 26 October saying he had “decided to use all air-defense means in the event of attack” is known only from the secondary accounts of Fursenko and Naftali and of Dobbs; its text has not been released. Whether the “order to fire at 20:34 on the 26th” in Garbuz’s testimony was Pliyev’s own discretion within the “joint repulse” framework of No. 4/389 of 22 October is not settled by the documents (Issue 2). The choices in this scene fill that gap.
note.src: Statsenko 1962; Garbuz 1992; Fursenko & Naftali [secondary]; Phase 1 issue 2

pressure.title: The Night the Cubans Fire
pressure.text: Alekseev’s message is plain. The Cuban leadership expects an air strike between tonight and tomorrow, and Castro has decided to open anti-aircraft fire if the attack comes. Fifty Cuban anti-aircraft batteries are already around the division, and their commanders are under orders not to fire unless attacked first. No. 4/389 told you to repel the enemy jointly with the Cubans but did not say whether air-defense fire was part of that, and if you ask Moscow, the answer takes a day. Garbuz will later testify that he received an order to fire at 8:34 that evening and say Pliyev had the authority to make such a decision, but the text of the cable you sent Moscow was never released. Grechko’s 24 S-75 battalions are all ready to fire, and if the Soviets fire, theirs will be the first Soviet missile to bring down an American plane. Between an ally’s honor and Moscow’s permission, the one sentence you write decides what happens tomorrow morning.
pressure.src: Statsenko 1962; Garbuz 1992; Fursenko & Naftali [secondary]; Wilson/UMD 111915 (English translation)

map.caption: The 24 S-75 surface-to-air missile battalions in Cuba were allowed to switch on their radars from 26 October, and on the morning of the 27th they shot down a U-2.

PL-05.time: About 2 a.m. (10 a.m. in Moscow, 3 a.m. in Washington)
PL-05.place: From the Group’s central nuclear warhead store to the launch area of Sidorov’s regiment, 500 kilometers
PL-05.title: Five Hundred Kilometers
PL-05.clock: About four hours until sunrise; Sidorov’s regiment needs 10 hours to prepare a launch
PL-05.event: That same night, in the Soviet embassy residence in Havana, Castro is dictating a letter to Khrushchev from 2 a.m. to 7 a.m.: the attack, it says, will come within 24 to 72 hours. The latter part of the letter calls for a Soviet response in the event of an invasion, and its meaning will later be read in two ways. You know nothing of the letter. In front of you is a plan for escorting the warheads.
PL-05.scene: Statsenko has come to see you in the night. The nuclear warheads are in the Group’s store, and the launch area of Sidorov’s regiment is 500 kilometers away. Send the warheads out after the order comes, and the road alone takes a day. He proposes moving them close to the launch area “with the aim of reducing the time needed to prepare the first salvo.” Beloborodov’s convoy cannot cover that distance before sunrise even driving through the night, so you must choose between nuclear warhead trucks passing under American reconnaissance planes in daylight and warheads arriving a day late when the landing comes. Garbuz goes back over the alert levels. The Group is at level four. If an order for level three comes, the warheads are assembled; without an order there is no authority to assemble them. Moving and assembling are different things, and a line runs between them. By the morning of 27 October all 24 of the division’s launchers will be ready to fire. Only Moscow can give the order to launch; where the warheads sit is for you to decide.

voices.who: Statsenko (commander, 51st Missile Division, report of December 1962)
voices.text: With the aim of reducing the time needed to prepare the first salvo.

voices.who: Garbuz (deputy commander for combat training, recalling in 1992)
voices.text: The nuclear warheads were a long way from the missiles. The commander allowed them to be moved closer. We were at the fourth level of readiness. If an order came down to go to the third level, we would assemble the warheads; without an order we had no authority to assemble them.

voices.who: Beloborodov (colonel, in charge of nuclear warhead storage and escort)
voices.text: Five hundred kilometers means we will still be on the road after sunrise. I will dress the convoy up as ordinary freight trucks. But assembly needs my signature and Moscow’s code. I will take an order to move them; assembly is another matter.

choices.text: Move the warheads, go to level three, and have them assembled. Once a landing starts there will be no time to ask Moscow
choices.why: A commander’s reckoning: a nuclear weapon that is not ready might as well not exist
choices.after: Beloborodov read the order twice and asked for a signature. You signed. The convoy left, and the assembly crews followed. Within hours that signature would collide with Moscow’s No. 76639.

choices.text: Leave the warheads in the store. A 500-kilometer night convoy would show American reconnaissance planes nuclear warheads on the move
choices.why: Not being found out is a greater safety than a day of preparation time
choices.after: Statsenko folded his map without a word. The division reported all 24 launchers ready to fire, but with the convoy time added, Sidorov’s regiment needed more than a day. In the morning a cable came from Moscow.

choices.text: Move Sidorov’s warheads from the store to the launch area. Stay at level four, and no assembly without an order from Moscow
choices.why: A commander’s compromise: cut the time, but do not cross the line
choices.after: The convoy set off into the night. On 27 October all 24 of the division’s launchers were ready to fire, and Sidorov’s regiment’s preparation time fell to 10 hours. The warheads were beside the launch area, unassembled. In the morning a cable came from Moscow.

note.text: Paragraphs 194–205 of Statsenko’s report record that on the night of 26–27 October the warheads of Sidorov’s regiment were moved 500 kilometers from the store to the launch area, and that on the 27th all 24 of the division’s launchers were ready to fire, with preparation times of 14–16 hours for Solovyov’s and Bandilovsky’s regiments and 10 hours for Sidorov’s. Garbuz testified that “the commander allowed them to be moved.” The location of the store is not confirmed in primary sources, so it is not named here.

map.caption: Warheads were moved from the central nuclear warhead store at Bejucal to the launch area of Sidorov’s regiment at Sagua la Grande, a distance the division’s report gives as 500 kilometers.

PL-06.time: 8:30 a.m. (4:30 p.m. in Moscow, 9:30 a.m. in Washington)
PL-06.title: No. 76639
PL-06.clock: Thirty minutes until Radio Moscow broadcasts Khrushchev’s letter (9 a.m. Havana)

telegram.subject: Reply to your No. 8/154
telegram.text: We categorically reaffirm that use of nuclear weapons from the missiles, the FKRs, the Lunas and the aircraft without orders from Moscow is forbidden. / Confirm receipt.

PL-06.event: Three cables have come in at once: No. 76639, reaffirming the ban on nuclear use; an order to halt all work on deploying the R-12s and R-14s and to camouflage at night; and a reply telling you to send the Aleksandrovsk home to the Soviet Union with the Bratsk. At the Presidium this morning Moscow decided to add the American missiles in Turkey to its terms, and it is putting the letter out on the radio at 5 p.m., Moscow time. Havana will hear what it says in thirty minutes.
PL-06.scene: You are unwell. You have been up for several nights running, you have a fever, and the doctor tells you to lie down. In that state you receive three cables. The first is the reply to your No. 8/154. Whether No. 8/154 reported the Cubans’ expectation of an air strike and your decision to open air-defense fire, or asked about the conditions for nuclear use, the answer is plain: nuclear use without orders from Moscow is “categorically” forbidden; confirm receipt. The second cable says to stop all work on deploying the missiles. It contains the sentence “You are provoking the UN.” Until last night the division was straining to bring its 24 launchers to readiness; now it is to stop, camouflage, and move only at night. Grechko has gone to the air-defense command post, and American aircraft have been showing on the radar since morning. You must write your acknowledgment and then decide where you will be.

voices.who: Malinovsky (Trostnik, cable of the same day)
voices.text: Halt all work on deploying the R-12s and R-14s. You are provoking the UN. Camouflage everything carefully and work only at night.

voices.who: Garbuz (deputy commander for combat training, recalling in 1992)
voices.text: No one but Moscow could change the level of readiness.

voices.who: Grechko (deputy commander for air defense, by telephone)
voices.text: Comrade Commander, a high-altitude target is coming up on the radar. We are tracking it as decided yesterday. Get some rest, Comrade Commander. I will call if I need you.

choices.text: Confirm receipt, then drag yourself to the air-defense command post. Whatever is decided over Cuba today, the commander decides it in person
choices.why: On a day when the responsibility is yours, you cannot leave it to a deputy on the telephone
choices.after: The acknowledgment went out, and you called for a car. When you walked into the air-defense command post, a single high-altitude target was crossing the island from the east on the screen. It had been tracked for an hour.

choices.text: Add one line to your acknowledgment, asking that authority to use the Lunas pass to the commander if a landing begins and contact with Moscow is lost
choices.why: Accept the ban, but fill the gap that opens once communications are cut
choices.after: The cable went out. Before any answer came, Garbuz recalled the wording of the draft instruction said to have been prepared in September: a landing and a concentration offshore, communications cut, the commander deciding on his own. You began to write a Group of Forces order in those words.

choices.text: Confirm receipt. Halt the work, order night camouflage, leave air-defense command to Grechko, and go back to your quarters
choices.why: The order is clear and you are only one man, so leave it to the chain of command
choices.after: The acknowledgment went out. Statsenko’s division stopped work and thickened its camouflage. You went back to your quarters and lay down. Less than two hours later Grechko knocked at the door.

note.text: No. 76639 replied to Pliyev’s No. 8/154, whose text has never been released anywhere. The words “categorically reaffirm” mean Moscow had sent the same ban before (No. 4/389 of 22 October). That day’s Moscow Presidium also had a separate document, an “instruction on Pliyev’s cable,” but this study could not decipher it. That Pliyev was ill that day comes from Garbuz’s testimony; he does not name the illness, so it is not named here.

pressure.title: The Morning of the Fever
pressure.text: No. 76639 is the reply to your No. 8/154: a single sentence categorically forbidding nuclear use without orders from Moscow, and a demand to confirm receipt. “Categorically reaffirm” means the same ban was sent before, which is to say Moscow read something in your cable. The second cable tells you to stop all work on deploying the missiles and adds that you are provoking the UN. The man who must give that order to a division that spent last night straining to bring 24 launchers to readiness is 58, has gone without sleep for several nights, and is running a fever; the doctor tells him to lie down. According to Garbuz, the tropical heat and the life of concealment since July had worn the body down. Where the commander is will decide who makes the decision over Cuba a few hours from now.

PL-07.time: About 10:30 a.m. (6:30 p.m. in Moscow, 11:30 a.m. in Washington)
PL-07.place: El Chico headquarters, the commander’s quarters
PL-07.title: The Guest
PL-07.clock: About sixteen hours until Malinovsky reports to Khrushchev (10:45 a.m. on the 28th, Moscow)
PL-07.event: Meanwhile the world moved on. At 4:30 p.m. Moscow time (8:30 a.m. in Havana) the cable reaffirming the nuclear ban reached you, and at 5 p.m. (9 a.m. in Havana) Khrushchev’s letter went out on the radio. At 10:20 a.m. Havana time (6:20 p.m. in Moscow) the 507th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment brought down a U-2 at 21,000 meters with two S-75s. The pilot, Major Anderson, came down near Antilla and was killed. Washington will learn of it an hour later and convene the ExComm at 4 p.m. The same day a U-2 out of Alaska strayed into Soviet airspace, and in the Caribbean B-59 is under depth charges.
PL-07.scene: Grechko and Garbuz come into your quarters. There was a guest, Grechko says. A high-altitude reconnaissance plane came in from the east and crossed the island for 1 hour 21 minutes, over the road the nuclear warhead convoy had taken. The commander was ill and could not be reached; the radar officer said the target would be back over Guantánamo in five minutes. Grechko decided to shoot it down, with Garbuz beside him. Both of us are responsible, he says. Two missiles from the 507th Regiment, 21,000 meters, down near Antilla. The pilot cannot have survived. No report has gone to Moscow yet. What it says is up to you. You can write that it was to keep the photographs from getting out; you can name who decided, or you can leave that out. And low-level reconnaissance planes keep coming into the sky. The decision to open air-defense fire made yesterday still stands.

voices.who: Grechko (deputy commander for air defense, as reported by Garbuz)
voices.text: Grechko said our guest had come. He said the commander was ill and could not be reported to. Still, he said, we have to shoot it down.

voices.who: Garbuz (deputy commander for combat training, recalling in 1992)
voices.text: The radar officer said that in five minutes the target would be back over Guantánamo. Grechko said he had decided to shoot it down. But we were both responsible.
Comrade Commander, low-flying aircraft have come over the division three times. The Cuban guns fired. No damage on our side; work is stopped and we are under camouflage.

choices.text: Report the shootdown to Moscow as it happened. Write that it was to keep the photographs from getting out, and do not say who gave the order
choices.why: The army’s old rule: a unit’s decision is its commander’s decision
choices.after: The report reached Moscow that night. At 10:45 a.m. on the 28th Malinovsky reported to Khrushchev that the plane had been shot down “to prevent the Americans from obtaining photographs.” That report, too, names no one who decided. American aircraft were counted as violating Cuban airspace eight times that day.

choices.text: Endorse Grechko’s decision and go a step further: authorize the S-75s and anti-aircraft guns to fire on low-level reconnaissance planes too
choices.why: A soldier’s logic: having brought down one, you must stop the rest or it means nothing
choices.after: In the afternoon two low-level reconnaissance planes came in, and one was hit by anti-aircraft fire and went into the sea. At that evening’s meeting in Washington the Joint Chiefs recommended attacking the surface-to-air missile sites the next morning, and this time the President did not put it off.

choices.text: Order the air-defense divisions to cease fire and name Grechko in the report as the one who decided. There must be no more launches the commander does not know about
choices.why: Only a clear record of where responsibility lies can stop the next launch
choices.after: Grechko saluted without a word and went out. The air-defense divisions were ordered to track only and lock their launchers. The report went to Moscow, and the answer that came back the next morning did not ask who had decided; it held a single sentence: “too hasty.”

note.text: Who ordered the U-2 shootdown is disputed. Garbuz (1992) testified that Pliyev was ill and absent, that Grechko decided, and that the two of them shared the responsibility. Malinovsky’s report of 28 October says only that the plane was shot down “to prevent the Americans from obtaining photographs” and names no one. Moscow’s rebuke went to Pliyev. Cuban anti-aircraft fire at low-flying planes that same day is in Castro’s letter of 28 October; the claim in Statsenko’s report of “an F-106 shot down” does not match American records. The Cubans had no part in the U-2 shootdown.

pressure.title: We Were Both Responsible
pressure.text: Grechko said there had been a guest, that the commander was ill and could not be reached, and that the radar officer said the target would be back over Guantánamo in five minutes. He decided to shoot it down, Garbuz was beside him, and both were responsible, they say. If the report to Moscow names who decided, two deputy commanders take the blame; if it does not, “Pavlov” takes it. Malinovsky’s report to Khrushchev the next morning said only that the 507th Regiment had fired two missiles to keep the Americans from obtaining photographs, and named no one. And the rebuke came to you. Between the army’s old rule that a unit’s decision is its commander’s, and not knowing how Moscow will take the shootdown, you must settle one line of the report.

PL-08.time: 8 a.m. (4 p.m. in Moscow, 9 a.m. in Washington) to 3 p.m.
PL-08.place: Group of Forces headquarters, El Chico
PL-08.title: Too Hasty
PL-08.clock: One hour until Radio Moscow broadcasts Khrushchev’s reply (9 a.m. Havana)

telegram.subject: U-2 shootdown and dismantling of the R-12s
telegram.text: We consider that you were too hasty in shooting down the American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft, at a time when an agreement to avert an attack on Cuba by peaceful means was taking shape. / Decision taken to dismantle the R-12s and remove them. Begin carrying out this measure. / Confirm receipt.

PL-08.event: Meanwhile the world moved on. That morning the Presidium at Novo-Ogaryovo outside Moscow decided to accept Kennedy’s letter of 27 October and dictated a reply announcing the dismantling. At 5 p.m. Moscow time (9 a.m. in Havana) the reply went out on the radio, and Castro heard it there. A few hours later Castro will announce his five points. In the Caribbean, B-59 has finished charging overnight and is trying to shake off its pursuers. At 10:30 a.m., Havana time, a second cable arrived, No. 4/835: on top of the ban on the S-75s, fighters are not to be scrambled either.
PL-08.scene: The first sentence of the cable is a rebuke; the second is withdrawal. The division that brought 24 launchers to readiness by yesterday morning must now take them apart and load them on ships. No one at headquarters says a word. Garbuz would later recall that the commander did not criticize them. There is no time to criticize anyone. At 9 a.m. Radio Moscow began reading Khrushchev’s reply in English, and someone in the signals room took it down: “a new order on the dismantling of the weapons which you describe as ‘offensive,’ and their crating and return to the Soviet Union.” Your order had arrived an hour ahead of Moscow’s radio. Ambassador Alekseev telephones with Castro’s reaction. Not relief but fury: Cuba has been made an article of trade without being consulted. Statsenko says dismantling will take three days. At 3 p.m. you must sign directive No. 7665. What more to put in it, or leave out, is still to be decided.

voices.text: In addition to the order not to use the S-75s, you are ordered not to scramble fighters, to avoid clashes with American reconnaissance aircraft.

voices.who: Garbuz (deputy commander for combat training, recalling in 1992)
voices.text: The commander did not criticize us.

We can finish dismantling between the 29th and the 31st. We leave the missiles as they are and strip the launchers and support equipment first. Moscow will set the loading schedule, I expect. The division will do as ordered.

Castro heard it on the radio. He is angry that he was not consulted, and within a few hours he will announce his own terms. The Cubans are going to see Soviet troops start taking the missiles apart, and I need your word, Comrade Commander, on how to explain that.

choices.text: Carry out the dismantling, but recommend separately to Moscow that the nuclear means of the Lunas, FKRs and Il-28s stay in Cuba
choices.why: Even if the strategic missiles go, the means to defend the island must stay
choices.after: Directive No. 7665 was issued at 3 p.m., and the recommendation went out that night. Moscow’s answer in early November went the way you wanted: the withdrawal of the Luna, FKR and Il-28 warheads was not yet under discussion, and they would stay in Cuba under your command. How that answer was reversed is the next scene.

choices.text: Send a separate report explaining how the shootdown happened, putting on record that it was a deputy’s decision in the commander’s absence
choices.why: The record decides where the rebuke should land
choices.after: The report went out and no answer came. That evening Moscow was absorbed in sending Castro a letter urging “patience, restraint and more restraint.” Dismantling began on the 29th and was finished on the 31st. Your report went into an archive somewhere, and Grechko later moved to another post.

choices.text: Issue directive No. 7665. Dismantle the launch sites and prepare the whole division to go home. Answer the rebuke with an acknowledgment and nothing more
choices.why: A soldier’s habit: an order is an order, and excuses do not go on the record
choices.after: At 3 p.m. directive No. 7665 was issued: launch sites to be dismantled, the whole division to return to the Soviet Union. The launchers came apart between 29 and 31 October, and on 1 November the Defense Ministry ordered loading to be completed between the 7th and the 10th. Cuban soldiers watched from the roadside.

note.text: The originals of Nos. 76645 and 4/835 are in the Wilson Center Digital Archive. The “too hasty” rebuke went to Pliyev, and Garbuz recalled that Moscow pressed them no further and that the commander did not criticize them either. Paragraphs 208–211 of Statsenko’s report record directive No. 7665 issued at 15:00 on 28 October, dismantling completed on the 29th–31st, and the Defense Ministry’s loading order at 12:00 on 1 November (for 7–10 November). The time Khrushchev’s reply was broadcast (17:00 Moscow) and the time Castro heard it in Havana (“around noon”) differ from account to account.

pressure.title: Too Hasty
pressure.text: The first sentence of No. 76645 rebukes you: shooting down the U-2 was too hasty. The second orders the R-12s dismantled and withdrawn. No. 4/835, which followed, added to the ban on the S-75s a ban on scrambling fighters. The division that brought 24 launchers to readiness by yesterday morning must take them apart and load them aboard ship within three days, while Khrushchev’s reply is being read in English on the radio. Castro’s reaction, as Alekseev relays it, is not relief but fury: Cuba has been made an article of trade without being consulted. Garbuz later recalled that Moscow pressed them no further and that the commander did not criticize his men either. On 21 November, at the Group’s military council, Mikoyan will say the missiles stood up like a parade on Red Square, and you will be the one listening.

PL-H1.time: About 9 a.m. (5 p.m. in Moscow, 10 a.m. in Washington)
PL-H1.place: El Chico headquarters, the commander’s office
PL-H1.title: The Commander’s Discretion
PL-H1.clock: Radio Moscow broadcasting Khrushchev’s letter at this very hour
PL-H1.scene: On your desk lies a draft Group of Forces order. It sets down, as Garbuz remembered it, the wording of the instruction said to have been prepared in Moscow on 8 September: if the enemy lands in Cuba, a landing fleet concentrates offshore and its destruction is delayed, and there is no way to receive instructions from the Soviet Defense Ministry, the commander may decide on his own to use the nuclear means of the Lunas, the Il-28s and the FKR-1s as instruments of local war. Only one copy of that instruction was made in Moscow, and it was never signed. What you hold is that memory transferred onto a Group of Forces order form. Beloborodov has said that assembling the warheads needs both his signature and Moscow’s code, and No. 76639 is in the signals room: “We categorically reaffirm that use without orders from Moscow is forbidden.” If you issue the order, the three Luna battalions and the FKR regiment will fire nuclear warheads on a word from you the moment the landing begins. If you do not, there will be nothing they can fire once the landing starts and the lines go dead. On the radio Khrushchev’s letter is being read in English. You hear the word Turkey.

voices.who: Malinovsky and Zakharov (draft instruction of 8 September, in substance)
voices.text: Should the enemy land and concentrate offshore so that his destruction is delayed, and there be no possibility of receiving instructions from the Defense Ministry, the commander may decide on his own to use the nuclear means of the Lunas, the Il-28s and the FKR-1s as instruments of local war. Single copy prepared; not signed by Malinovsky.

voices.who: Beloborodov (colonel, in charge of nuclear warhead storage and escort)
voices.text: Comrade Commander, without my signature the warheads are not assembled. And my signature comes only with Moscow’s code. If you tell me to sign a commander’s order, I will have to report it to Moscow.

When the landing comes, the first thing they hit is the signals center. No one here believes we will be able to ask Moscow then. But No. 76639 came this morning. You would be laying a commander’s order on top of that cable.

choices.text: Issue the order to the three Luna battalions and the FKR regiment: if landing forces come ashore and contact with Moscow is lost, prepare to launch on the commander’s order
choices.why: Resolved that the commander must fill the void once communications are cut
choices.after: The order went to every battalion. Beloborodov signed, saying he would report it to Moscow, and you told him to go ahead. That night an American reconnaissance plane came down, and by the next morning the sky had changed.

choices.text: Put the draft in the safe. Tell your deputies that as long as No. 76639 stands, no commander’s order can move the nuclear means
choices.why: An unsigned memory cannot override a signed ban
choices.after: The document went into the safe, and you went back to your quarters and lay down. Less than two hours later Grechko knocked at the door. There had been a guest, he said.

choices.text: Issue no order, but send the warheads up to the Luna battalions with assembly crews attached. Whether to use them, the commander will decide then
choices.why: A compromise: put off the decision, but make sure a decision can be made
choices.after: The warhead convoy went to the Luna battalions. Nothing was assembled, and the assembly crews slept beside the warheads. That night an American reconnaissance plane came down, and by the next morning the sky had changed.

note.text: This scene imagines the draft instruction of 8 September revived as a Group of Forces order. In fact Major General Yeliseyev wrote out a single copy of the draft and showed it to Lieutenant General Davidkov, and Malinovsky did not sign it. General Gribkov said at the 1992 Havana conference that authority had been delegated, but No. 4/389 of 22 October and No. 76639 of 27 October put the opposite on paper.

PL-H2.time: 10:15 a.m. (6:15 p.m. in Moscow, 11:15 a.m. in Washington)
PL-H2.place: El Chico headquarters, air-defense command post
PL-H2.title: Five Minutes
PL-H2.clock: Five minutes until the target slips away toward Guantánamo
PL-H2.scene: The target on the screen is circling the east of the island at more than 20,000 meters. It has been tracked for 1 hour 20 minutes. Its track overlaps the road the nuclear warhead convoy took. That plane is carrying the photographs. The radar officer says: in five minutes it will be back over Guantánamo. Grechko looks at you. Yesterday’s decision to open air-defense fire still stands, and two S-75s of the 507th Regiment are on their launchers. Fire, and it will be the first time Soviet forces have brought down an American aircraft, and the pilot will not survive. Hold fire, and the photographs of the convoy go to Washington. This morning Moscow’s No. 76639 was about nuclear weapons and said nothing about the S-75s. There is no time to ask Moscow. You are here because you chose to be.

voices.who: Grechko (deputy commander for air defense, as reported by Garbuz)
voices.text: Still, we have to shoot it down.

voices.who: Garbuz (deputy commander for combat training, recalling in 1992)
voices.text: Nuclear weapons were being transported, and they could see them.
Target turning, altitude twenty-one thousand, leaving airspace in five minutes. 507th Regiment holding track, standing by to launch.

choices.text: Order the 507th Regiment to fire. You cannot let the warhead convoy be photographed, and yesterday’s decision to fire was the commander’s own
choices.why: A commander who has made a decision follows it through to the end
choices.after: Two missiles went up. At 10:20 the target vanished from the screen and came down near Antilla. You reported to Moscow that it had been shot down to keep the photographs from getting out. This time the report named who had decided. It named you.

choices.text: Hold fire. A shootdown without Moscow’s permission is a heavier burden than one set of photographs. Track it on radar and let it go
choices.why: No one knows how far the death of one pilot might spread
choices.after: Five minutes later the target disappeared toward Guantánamo. Grechko ordered the missiles taken down from the launchers. That afternoon Washington’s meeting took place with no plane shot down, and how much difference that made would show the next morning.

choices.text: Scramble MiG-21s to shadow the target. Do not shoot it down, but show that the sky over Cuba is not empty
choices.why: A compromise: there is a way to warn without firing
choices.after: Two MiGs went up but could not reach a target at 20,000 meters. The target slipped away toward Guantánamo, and the MiGs came back. The next day Moscow sent a cable forbidding fighter sorties too.

note.text: According to Garbuz, Pliyev was in fact absent at this hour, and the shootdown was Grechko’s decision. This scene imagines Pliyev at the command post. The U-2’s altitude of 21,000 meters is in Malinovsky’s report of 28 October, and Cuba’s MiG-21s are known to have been unable to climb that high (published specifications, secondary). No. 4/835 of 28 October did in fact forbid fighter sorties.

PL-H3.time: Dawn (afternoon in Moscow, dawn in Washington)
PL-H3.place: Forward command post of a Luna battalion, north coast of Cuba
PL-H3.title: The Landing
PL-H3.clock: Tens of minutes until the first landing craft reach the beach; six hours since contact with Moscow was lost
PL-H3.scene: For two days, 28 and 29 October, American air strikes went on, hitting the missile sites and the surface-to-air missile bases one after another. Statsenko’s division has lost half its launchers, and most of the air-defense divisions’ radars are dark. Then, at dawn today, a fleet appeared on the horizon off the north coast. Landing craft are being lowered. The signals center was wrecked in yesterday’s bombing, the backup links are drowned in jamming, and you have been cut off from Moscow for six hours. Cuban divisions hold the coastal positions, with the four Soviet regiments behind them. The Luna battalion’s launchers are beside you, and the warheads are assembled or waiting to be. The order you gave on 27 October, or did not give, takes effect here. A single Luna nuclear warhead can wipe out one landing beach. No one knows what comes after. Garbuz asks: Comrade Commander, your orders.

voices.text: The landing craft are coming in. Conventional warheads will hold only one corner of the beach. On your order, Comrade Commander, the Lunas can fire within twenty minutes. Without it, we fight with conventional weapons and get pushed back.

voices.who: Beloborodov (colonel, in charge of nuclear warhead storage and escort)
voices.text: We are cut off from Moscow. I will sign if you give the order, Comrade Commander. I will only say that what follows that signature, no one can undo.

voices.who: Alekseev (ambassador to Cuba, last telephone call)
voices.text: Castro is at his command post. The Cubans will fight to the end. He has not told the Soviet forces to use the means they have, but he has not told them not to, either.

choices.text: Fire the Lunas with conventional warheads only. No nuclear use until contact with Moscow is restored; the four Soviet regiments fight on the beaches alongside the Cubans
choices.why: Losing communications does not mean the orders have changed
choices.after: Conventional Luna rounds fell on the beaches, and the landing was slowed but not stopped. The Soviet regiments fought alongside the Cubans as they fell back. When contact with Moscow was restored three days later, the first cable reaffirmed the ban on nuclear use.

choices.text: Order the Lunas to fire, with nuclear warheads, on the landing beach. Cut off from Moscow, this is the only means left to hold the island
choices.why: Resolved that an army sent to defend Cuba cannot leave unused what it holds in its hands
choices.after: The Luna left its launcher. A flash rose over the landing beach, and no one in Cuba was able to give a full account of what followed. How Washington and Moscow read that flash, you will see in the Ending.

choices.text: Strike the landing fleet and Guantánamo together with FKR nuclear warheads. The landing ends only when the fleet, not the beach, is destroyed
choices.why: A soldier’s logic: once you decide to use it, you see it through
choices.after: The FKR cruise missiles flew toward the sea and the base at the island’s eastern tip. Flashes rose over the fleet and the base, and once the news reached Washington, what followed was no longer Cuba’s affair.

note.text: The American OPLAN 316 assumed a landing within seven days of the air strikes, and on the evening of 27 October the Joint Chiefs recommended an air strike on Monday followed by an invasion. The tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba were 12 Luna warheads, 80 FKR warheads and 6 Il-28 bombs (Savranskaya 2012; consistent with the withdrawal order of 20 November). On 30 October Khrushchev wrote to Castro that proposing a nuclear first strike had been “wrong.” The landing and the communications breakdown in this scene are hypothetical.

map.caption: The two FKR cruise-missile regiments were near Mariel in the west and at Mayarí Arriba in the east, and the Mayarí Arriba unit was aimed at the Guantánamo base.

PL-H4.time: 9 a.m. (5 p.m. in Moscow, 10 a.m. in Washington)
PL-H4.place: Signals room, Group of Forces headquarters, El Chico
PL-H4.title: A Morning Without a Shootdown
PL-H4.clock: Radio Moscow’s broadcast beginning at this very hour

telegram.subject: Dismantling of the R-12s
telegram.text: Decision taken to dismantle the R-12s and remove them. Begin carrying out this measure. / Do not use the S-75s. To avoid clashes with American reconnaissance aircraft, do not scramble fighters either. / Confirm receipt.

PL-H4.scene: Yesterday that plane went back to Guantánamo, and Washington’s evening meeting took place without a downed pilot. This morning Moscow’s cable carries no rebuke, only the order to dismantle. On the radio Khrushchev’s reply is being read in English: a new order has been given to dismantle the weapons you call offensive and return them to the Soviet Union. Headquarters is quiet. No one asks whether holding fire yesterday was right, but everyone is thinking it. Garbuz asks: Comrade Commander, if we had fired yesterday, how would this cable be different? You do not answer. Statsenko says dismantling will take three days, and Alekseev reports that Castro heard it on the radio. The work is the same as it would have been; the only difference is a missing sentence of rebuke.

voices.text: We will finish dismantling between the 29th and the 31st. We leave the missiles themselves as they are and strip the launchers and support equipment first.
Castro heard it on the radio. He is angry that he was not consulted, and within a few hours he will announce his own terms.
The air-defense divisions go back to the ban on firing. Garbuz and I will both remember that it was you, Comrade Commander, who made the decision in those five minutes yesterday.

choices.text: Carry out the dismantling, but recommend separately to Moscow that the nuclear means of the Lunas, FKRs and Il-28s stay in Cuba
choices.why: Even if the strategic missiles go, the means to defend the island must stay
choices.after: The directive was issued at 3 p.m., and the recommendation went out that night. Moscow’s answer in early November was that the tactical nuclear warheads would stay in Cuba under your command.

choices.text: Issue the directive and begin dismantling the launch sites. Return the air-defense divisions to the ban on firing and send back an acknowledgment, nothing more
choices.why: When the order is clear, the commander’s only task is to carry it out
choices.after: At 3 p.m. the directive was issued. The launchers came apart between the 29th and the 31st. The only people who know that Moscow’s cable lacked the words “too hasty” are you and your two deputies.

note.text: The cable in this scene is hypothetical: the real Nos. 76645 and 4/835 with the sentence rebuking the U-2 shootdown removed, set out as a single cable. How Washington’s evening meeting would have gone had there been no shootdown on 27 October is conjecture. The Joint Chiefs cited that day’s shootdown in recommending an attack on the surface-to-air missile sites the next morning, and the President put it off.

PL-H5.time: 6 a.m. (2 p.m. in Moscow, 7 a.m. in Washington)
PL-H5.place: Group of Forces headquarters, El Chico, air-defense command post
PL-H5.title: The Retaliatory Strike
PL-H5.clock: Two hours until contact with Moscow is possible; no telling when the next wave comes
PL-H5.scene: They came before sunrise. American aircraft out of Guantánamo and Florida struck the surface-to-air missile sites and anti-aircraft positions that fired yesterday. The 507th Regiment’s launchers are wrecked and two radars are dark. After you authorized fire on low-flying planes yesterday, one was hit by anti-aircraft fire and went into the sea, and overnight Washington cited it in deciding on a retaliatory strike. The strike spared the missile sites. For now. In the air-defense command post Grechko is calling out the state of the surviving battalions, and Garbuz says contact with Moscow is two hours away. You must decide whether to answer with conventional air defense, switch off the radars and disperse to wait out the next strike, or move the Luna battalions forward against a landing. Khrushchev’s reply is due on the radio in three hours, but even Moscow does not know whether it will say the same thing after this morning’s strike.

voices.text: Eighteen battalions left, ready to fire. If they send a second wave, the target will be the missile sites. Give me the order to return fire and this time we shoot without warning.
The launch sites have not been hit yet. Sidorov’s regiment can fire within 10 hours. But only Moscow can give the order to fire, and we will not get through to Moscow for another two hours.

After the air strike comes the landing. That is how their plan will be laid out. If we move the Luna battalions forward to the north coast, we can fire on the landing, with conventional rounds if nothing else.

choices.text: Return fire with every air-defense means and move the Luna battalions forward to the north coast. Ask Moscow about nuclear use in the event of a landing
choices.why: An army that takes a beating without firing back invites the next strike
choices.after: The S-75s fired on the second wave and brought down two American planes. The launch sites were hit too. Two hours later Moscow sent a cable reaffirming the ban on nuclear use; it was the last cable received before the signals center was destroyed. Two days later a fleet appeared off the north coast.

choices.text: Switch off the radars and disperse the air-defense divisions. Report to Moscow, and do not return fire without orders
choices.why: On the first morning of air strikes, the Soviet forces’ task is to survive and report
choices.after: The radars went dark and the battalions scattered. The second wave hit the launch sites. Moscow’s cable said not to return fire and to disperse, and that evening Khrushchev’s reply went out as planned, but Washington had already moved on to the next stage.

choices.text: Order the FKR regiment to prepare a strike on Guantánamo, with conventional warheads, to put out of action the runway the American planes fly from
choices.why: A soldier’s reckoning: hitting where the strikes start is quicker than air defense
choices.after: Conventional FKR rounds fell on the Guantánamo runway. The strikes kept coming from Florida, and news that Soviet forces had attacked an American base reached Washington’s morning meeting. Two days later a fleet appeared off the north coast.

note.text: At the ExComm on the evening of 27 October, General Taylor, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, recommended attacking the surface-to-air missile sites the next morning, and the President put it off until Monday. This scene imagines that, with a low-flying plane also hit, the attack was not put off. On 22 October Khrushchev told the Presidium, “If they attack, we will respond,” and on the morning of 28 October he said he had “given the order for a retaliatory strike if an attack is provoked.”

PL-H6.time: Afternoon (night in Moscow, evening in Washington)
PL-H6.place: Group of Forces headquarters, El Chico
PL-H6.title: The Warheads to Keep
PL-H6.clock: Eleven days until the Atkarsk sails (1 December)

telegram.subject: Luna, FKR and aircraft nuclear warheads
telegram.text: Luna and FKR missiles with conventional warheads to remain in Cuba. / Send 6 nuclear bombs, 12 Luna warheads and 80 FKR warheads to the Soviet Union aboard the Atkarsk.

PL-H6.event: On 2 November First Deputy Premier Mikoyan arrived in Havana. On 5 November Moscow told you that the Luna, FKR and Il-28 warheads, “whose withdrawal has not yet been discussed, are to remain in Cuba under your command.” The conventional Lunas and FKRs were expected to be handed over to the Cubans, and Moscow asked your view on the timetable for the handover. Then, in mid-November, Moscow learned that Castro had instructed Ambassador Lechuga in New York that “Cuba has tactical nuclear weapons and must keep them.” Today in Washington Kennedy announces the lifting of the blockade, and the same day a cable comes from Moscow.
PL-H6.scene: The cable of 5 November and the cable of 20 November lie side by side on your desk. In two weeks Moscow has changed its mind. Mikoyan is about to tell Castro that a Soviet law forbids transferring nuclear weapons to a third country; there is no such law. The conventional Lunas and FKRs stay, and the nuclear warheads all go aboard the Atkarsk and leave on 1 December: 12 Luna warheads, 80 FKR warheads, 6 Il-28 bombs. These are the things you recommended keeping on 28 October. The conventional Lunas and FKRs were expected to go to the Cubans, and the Cuban leadership knows what kind of warheads these are. Beloborodov says it will take ten days to prepare the loading. You must decide one of two things: load them as ordered, or ask again about the handover timetable. Either way, the missiles have already gone, and the Soviet force left in Cuba is the size of one brigade.

voices.text: As for the warheads for the Lunas, the FKRs and the Il-28 aircraft, their withdrawal has not yet been discussed. They are to be kept in Cuba under your command.

Castro would not see Mikoyan for three days. He did agree to give up even the Il-28s, but since he knows the tactical nuclear weapons are here, he will ask whether those are going too. Mikoyan will answer that there is a law.

voices.who: Beloborodov (colonel, in charge of nuclear warhead storage and escort)
voices.text: Ten days to count and load ninety-eight. I will keep the Cubans away from the warhead store. But they already know what is in it.

choices.text: Keep preparing to hand the conventional Lunas and FKRs over to the Cubans, and cable Moscow asking again about a timetable for handing over the warheads
choices.why: A last attempt to make Moscow remember its promise of 5 November
choices.after: The answer was short: carry out the order of 20 November. On 1 December the Atkarsk sailed with 98 nuclear warheads aboard, and on 22 November Mikoyan told Castro about a law that did not exist. Castro asked when it would be repealed.

choices.text: As ordered, load the 6 nuclear bombs, 12 Luna warheads and 80 FKR warheads aboard the Atkarsk. The conventional Lunas and FKRs stay
choices.why: Nuclear weapons left in Cuba would be a burden to Moscow and Cuba alike
choices.after: On 1 December the Atkarsk sailed. Even then the United States did not know there had been tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba; it learned only after General Gribkov spoke of them at the 1992 Havana conference. The conventional Lunas and FKRs stayed with the Cubans.

note.text: The two cables, of around 5 November and of 20 November, are real documents. The scene is hypothetical because it supposes that Pliyev’s recommendation of 28 October prompted the decision to keep the tactical nuclear weapons; in fact that decision came from Moscow. That Castro’s instruction to Lechuga prompted the withdrawal is Savranskaya’s interpretation (secondary). The “law” Mikoyan cited on 22 November did not exist.

epilogues.A: The 51st Missile Division sailed between 7 and 10 November, and the nuclear warheads went home aboard the Atkarsk on 1 December. Pliyev stayed in Cuba until May 1963, cut the Group of Forces down to a brigade, and then returned to command the North Caucasus Military District; he died in Moscow in 1979. On 21 November Mikoyan told the Group’s military council that “the missiles stood up like a parade on Red Square.” At that same hour, in Kennedy’s room, the ExComm sat over the Il-28s and inspection after the blockade was lifted.
epilogues.B: The air strikes wiped out the missile sites, and within three days the landing was off the beaches. The four Soviet regiments fought alongside the Cubans as they fell back, and Moscow began to look for its answer in Berlin. Pliyev went into the record as the commander who did not use nuclear weapons, but that did not stop the war.
epilogues.C: Once the flash of the FKRs rose over the fleet and Guantánamo, what followed was no longer the affair of one island. Washington read it as a Soviet nuclear attack, and the decisions of the next few hours shaped the world that came after. That there had been 98 nuclear warheads in Cuba was the last thing the world learned that night.
epilogues.G: A single Luna wiped out the landing beach, and the Americans halted where they stood. Washington chose not to read it as the start of all-out nuclear war, and Moscow gave no order for a retaliatory strike. Pliyev remained the commander who had made that decision, and Cuba became the third place on earth where a nuclear weapon had been used.

dossier.t: Born in November 1903 the son of an Ossetian peasant in Stariy Batakoyurt, a mountain village in North Ossetia, he is 58 in October 1962. He joined the Red Army in 1922 and spent his whole career in the cavalry. In the war he led a cavalry corps and then a cavalry-mechanized group, winning his first Hero of the Soviet Union in the Odessa operation of 1944 and his second after commanding the Soviet-Mongolian cavalry-mechanized group in Manchuria in August 1945. Since 1958 he has commanded the North Caucasus Military District, and early in June 1962, at Novocherkassk, district troops opened fire on workers protesting wages and prices and killed 24; it happened inside your district. In July the Presidium sent you to Cuba instead of a rocket-forces general for the sake of cover, and you have never commanded missile troops. On paper you are “Pavlov,” and Moscow’s cables come under that name. You are a soldier of few words who starts with the order number and the time, and you are said to be strict but a commander who does not pass the blame. The tropical heat is hard on a body your age.

Major General Statsenko, commander of the 51st Missile Division, is bent on bringing his 24 R-12 launchers to readiness a day sooner, and he will be the first to suggest moving sites at night or keeping the warheads close to them. Lieutenant General Grechko, deputy for air defense, has 24 S-75 battalions, and when you are away the air-defense decisions are his. Major General Garbuz, deputy for combat training, came in with you in the July advance party and stays at your side at headquarters. Colonel Beloborodov is in charge of storing and escorting the nuclear warheads, which Moscow’s cables call “Beloborodov’s cargo,” and he says they cannot be assembled without an order from Moscow. In Havana, Ambassador Alekseev sees Castro on easy terms and brings you the Cuban leadership’s expectation of an air strike and its decisions to open anti-aircraft fire. In Moscow, Defense Minister Malinovsky sends coded cables under the name “Trostnik”; they are always short and always end with “Confirm receipt.”

Your greatest fear is the gap in your orders. On 8 September Moscow prepared an instruction that, if the enemy landed and communications were cut, the commander could decide on his own to use the nuclear means of the Lunas, the Il-28s and the FKRs; but the document was never signed, and only one copy is left. No document says what you may do when a landing fleet appears off the north coast and Moscow cannot be heard. Your second fear is Castro. The Cuban army is already fully mobilized and has moved 50 anti-aircraft batteries around the missile units, and every day, through Alekseev, comes the pressure: if the Cubans fire and the Soviets stay silent, this is no alliance. The third is Moscow’s silence. You are told nothing of what the Presidium discusses; what comes is short orders and reprimands. Your hope is that the Americans do not land, and that your 42,000 men and the nuclear warheads leave this island without a single round fired.

movers.intro: Whether Pliyev had the authority to use nuclear weapons on his own, and who decided to shoot down the U-2 on 27 October, are questions still unsettled even since the Soviet documents were opened in the 1990s. The main views are these:
views: Anatoli Gribkov and William Smith: at the 1992 Havana conference Gribkov said Pliyev had been delegated authority to use tactical nuclear weapons in the event of a landing, and in their 1994 book they printed the draft instruction of 8 September as evidence. This testimony that Moscow had placed nuclear decisions in Cuba became the starting point for every argument that followed.

Mark Kramer: drawing on the released cables, he rebuts Gribkov. The 8 September draft was never signed, No. 4/389 of 22 October excluded nuclear means, and No. 76639 of 27 October firmly restated the ban, so on the documents there was no valid delegation.

Aleksandr Fursenko and Timothy Naftali: from the Presidium records they show that on the night of 22 October Khrushchev spoke of allowing tactical nuclear use but Malinovsky stopped him, and they see Pliyev’s report to Moscow on 26 October that he had decided to use all air-defense means in the event of attack as the background to the next day’s shootdown.

Michael Dobbs: he accepts the testimony that Pliyev was ill and absent on the morning of 27 October and that Grechko and Garbuz decided on the shootdown, and, together with the move of an FKR cruise-missile unit toward Guantánamo that same night, he stresses that commanders on the ground made decisions beyond Moscow’s control.
movers.note: The texts of Pliyev’s cables of 26 and 27 October (Nos. 8/154 and 8/162) have not been released, and the Presidium’s “instruction on Pliyev’s cable” of 27 October has not been deciphered. Savranskaya links the story of how tactical nuclear weapons nearly stayed in Cuba in November to Castro’s instructions to Lechuga.
